{"id": "36:14/q11", "question": "What does the omitted object of fa-ʿazzaznā refer to?", "turns_on": "Whether the verb describes support of the two, support of the message, or victory over those who denied it.", "positions": [{"id": "36:14/q11/p1", "position": "It refers to the first two messengers, supplied by the preceding clause.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari and al-Nasafi say omission draws attention to Shimon and the subtle strategy by which truth prevailed; al-Zamakhshari compares omitting those judged when saying a ruler judged justly. Al-Baydawi says the context supplies the object and focuses on the helper. Abu Hayyan says the third reinforced the two and all prevailed through argument and tactful invitation. Bursevi and al-Alusi likewise recover the pair; al-Samin extends the omission to both readings."}, {"id": "36:14/q11/p2", "position": "The mission or call, rather than the messengers personally, is what was strengthened.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj says the message was reinforced; al-Samarrai explicitly distinguishes the call from the persons. Al-Wahidi prefers this explanation for the passage."}, {"id": "36:14/q11/p3", "position": "On the overcoming sense, the understood object is the opponents or the disbelievers.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi treat the third as the means of victory; Abu Ali says his proof defeated the opponents. Al-Samin's general statement instead calls the omitted object the two messengers even for the 'overcome' reading."}]}
{"id": "36:14/q12", "question": "Was the third sent after the pair or had he been sent earlier?", "turns_on": "Narrative order and whether 'third' can designate a man dispatched earlier but introduced after the pair.", "positions": [{"id": "36:14/q12/p1", "position": "The third was sent after the first two were rejected, to support them.", "reasons": "The sequence is explicit for Yahya ibn Sallam, Qatada, al-Tabari, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi and others; Wahb says the third received news of the imprisoned pair and set out. Al-Samarrai explains why the verse does not simply say three were sent at once. Ibn al-Jawzi objects that a messenger sent before both would be called first, and al-Nahhas says the apparent wording favors a later third; al-Tabataba'i rejects transmitted versions that jar with Quranic sequence."}, {"id": "36:14/q12/p2", "position": "The third had been sent before the pair; the narration mentions him later and speaks retrospectively of his strengthening.", "reasons": "Al-Farra identifies this earlier messenger as Shimon and says the strengthening came from what he taught the pair. Al-Nahhas reports his view but says an earlier man should have been introduced as 'the third' with the article. Ibn al-Jawzi rejects it because exegetes place the third later and because one sent first would not be third."}]}
{"id": "36:14/q13", "question": "Who is the third?", "turns_on": "Incompatible name traditions and, for Islahi and al-Qashani, different identifications of the entire parable.", "positions": [{"id": "36:14/q13/p1", "position": "He was Shimʿūn/Simon, also called al-Ṣafā, al-Ṣakhra or al-Ṣaffār, Jesus's disciple or successor.", "reasons": "Muqatil's form Shamʿūn/Shaman and many other reports identify Simon; Ibn Abbas calls him al-Ṣafā. Al-Qurtubi calls him chief of the apostles and says he entered the royal court in disguise. Bursevi calls him their leader and Jesus's successor after the ascension. Al-Durr mentions a messengerless interval of 434 years. In one report God inspired him with the pair's plight; in others Jesus sent him. Al-Farra instead puts Simon before the pair. Elmalili's reported John–Paul pair makes Simon Peter third."}, {"id": "36:14/q13/p2", "position": "He was Salūm/Shalūm.", "reasons": "The Ibn Abbas–Ka'b–Wahb or Ka'b reports pair him with Ṣādiq and Ṣadūq; spelling varies."}, {"id": "36:14/q13/p3", "position": "He was Būluṣ/Paul.", "reasons": "Shuʿayb al-Jubbāʾī, Shu'ba and other reports pair him with Simon and John; al-Alusi notes a spelling with ṣād or sīn. Sa'id ibn Jubayr also names Paul, though he calls Simon son of John the helper and says all three were killed."}, {"id": "36:14/q13/p4", "position": "He was Yūnus/Jonas.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi attributes Yūnus to Shuʿayb; Study Quran reports Jonas as another identification; al-Alusi says Wahb and Ka'b also transmit Yūnus."}, {"id": "36:14/q13/p5", "position": "He was Pharaoh's believing kinsman who defended Moses, though not a prophet in the technical sense.", "reasons": "Islahi identifies him with the believer of 40:28 and the speaker in 40:26–45. He hid his faith until Pharaoh proposed killing Moses, then defended Moses before the court; his family status gave his plea force. His arguments and courage earn him collective inclusion with Moses and Aaron, as a member of one embassy can speak with the others; Islahi compares him with Abu Bakr among Muhammad's followers."}, {"id": "36:14/q13/p6", "position": "In an inward reading, the third is intellect, joining spirit and heart.", "reasons": "Al-Qashani says intellect shares the self's interests and succeeds in influencing it toward what heart and spirit seek, whereas the body initially rejects spirit and heart because of its darkness and lack of affinity."}]}
{"id": "36:14/q14", "question": "How does Arabic form and use ordinal expressions such as 'a third'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:14/q14/p1", "position": "Ordinals use the fāʿil pattern, with count, gender and compound-number forms governed by Arabic usage.", "reasons": "Sibawayh cites ثاني اثنين (9:40) and ثالث ثلاثة (5:73) for ordinals two through ten in annexation; feminine fāʿila takes a feminine ending, while feminine counted numbers three through ten omit hāʾ. خامس أربعة means making four into five and is rare though analogical; Arabic does not say ثاني واحد. Eleven through nineteen have open compound parts, as حادي عشر and ثالث عشر; feminine حادية عشرة follows its feminine number pattern. He treats خامس خمسة عشر and حادي أحد عشر, explaining when حادي declines, and notes a less common expanded ثالث عشر ثلاثة عشر whose final count is often omitted. Masculine ordinals dominate mixed-gender counts; خامس أربع for four women plus a man is scarcely used; higher patterns include رابع ثلاثة عشر and بضعة عشر/بضعة عشرة inflect like تسعة عشر/تسع عشرة."}]}
{"id": "36:14/q15", "question": "Is 'with a third' also read with a definite article?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:14/q15/p1", "position": "The transmitted wording is 'with the third' (bi-l-thālith).", "reasons": "Al-Farra attributes it to Abd Allah and explains definiteness by prior mention of the messengers, comparing 'the two dirhams' after an earlier reference. Ibn Atiyya identifies Ibn Masud's codex; al-Samin and al-Alusi also report Abd Allah's reading. Al-Nahhas says this would have been the natural wording for al-Farra's theory that the third had been sent first."}]}
{"id": "36:14/q16", "question": "What purpose or effect did sending a third serve?", "turns_on": "The literal mission, Islahi's Moses reading, or al-Qashani's inward reading determines the kind of support.", "positions": [{"id": "36:14/q16/p1", "position": "It reinforced the first two, increased their number, and made the proof and mission stronger.", "reasons": "Abu al-Aliya explicitly calls the third a stronger proof against the town; Ibn Zayd says making three is reinforcement. Ibn Atiyya says it completed the proof. Al-Biqa'i says God brought might to His cause after their weakening by denial. Al-Samarrai says rejection explains why support came later rather than all three at once. Al-Jishumi says one messenger may permissibly be strengthened by another; messengers sent together may share a law, while successively arriving messengers each require a new miracle and renewed law."}, {"id": "36:14/q16/p2", "position": "The third's fearless defense of Moses is the assistance celebrated by God's wording.", "reasons": "Islahi calls the defender of 40:26–45 courageous and unmatched outside prophets and the righteous. Pharaoh proposed killing Moses and charged him with changing religion; Moses sought protection; the believer argued that a true messenger's warnings could fall on them, invoked earlier ruined peoples, Joseph's signs and the Day of Flight, and warned against tyranny. Pharaoh claimed sound guidance and ordered Haman's tower. The believer's royal status and concealed faith made his public defense forceful."}, {"id": "36:14/q16/p3", "position": "The third's intellect mediated the inward call of spirit and heart to the self.", "reasons": "Al-Qashani says the body rejects spirit and heart because of opposed light and darkness; its bad omen is an aversion to discipline and spiritual struggle, and its stoning and torment of them are bodily impulses and animal appetites."}]}
{"id": "36:14/q17", "question": "What is reported about the envoys' encounter with Ḥabīb?", "turns_on": "Reports differ over how many believed and over the later fate of Habib and the envoys.", "positions": [{"id": "36:14/q17/p1", "position": "The envoys met Ḥabīb the shepherd or carpenter, cured his sick son and others, and he believed.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari says they met the carpenter tending goats near the city; Habib requested a sign, and the sick, blind and leprous, including a son ill for two years, were healed. Al-Qurtubi calls Habib the shepherd of a few sheep and identifies him with the man from the far end of town; his son is described as ill or possessed. Al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi and al-Tabataba'i recount the son's healing; al-Nasafi says he rose after their touch. News of many healings reached the king."}, {"id": "36:14/q17/p2", "position": "Only Ḥabīb al-Najjār believed; he left his work, later urged the townspeople to follow the messengers, and was killed.", "reasons": "Muqatil calls him an Israelite and former polytheist. Ibn Atiyya says a running believer was killed while the people persisted; Sa'id ibn Jubayr says Hab

ib had concealed his faith, all three envoys were killed, and Habib was then killed in a well at al-Rass. Ibn Ishaq's version has Habib run from the city's far gate when the king and people resolve to kill the envoys. Kuranyolu treats his likely murder as part of the warning."}]}
{"id": "36:14/q18", "question": "How did the envoys and their helper present signs to the king?", "turns_on": "The reported sign narratives differ in the person revived and in what the signs establish about the envoys' status.", "positions": [{"id": "36:14/q18/p1", "position": "They healed a blind boy and revived a child dead seven days, exposing the idols' powerlessness.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari describes Simon's disguise and court friendship, his challenge to the king's idol, the blind boy's missing eyes restored through prayer and two clay pellets, and revival after a seven-day death. The revived boy warned of seven valleys of Fire and said a handsome youth interceded for the three in heaven. Al-Qurtubi says the envoys prayed openly while Simon prayed secretly and the boy testified to God, Jesus and the envoys, naming Simon best; al-Tabrisi, al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi tell related versions. Al-Baydawi and al-Nasafi say the king admitted his idols neither hear, see, harm nor benefit. Abu Hayyan cites healing the blind and lepers and raising the dead as signs of clear delivery. Al-Biqa'i says messengers are accompanied by credible signs and cites Tufayl ibn Amr's requested light first on his forehead, then his whip."}, {"id": "36:14/q18/p2", "position": "Shamʿūn revived a girl from her grave before the people.", "reasons": "Muqatil says he struck the grave with his foot, called her by God's permission, and she emerged testifying that the emissaries were sent. She warned that acceptance brings forgiveness and refusal punishment, predicted disbelief, then returned to her grave at her request."}, {"id": "36:14/q18/p3", "position": "Miracle reports may be Jesus's confirming wonder through the apostles, rather than proof they were prophets.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi records this answer to the claim that only prophets properly have miracles; the apostles may have spoken as direct envoys or representatives."}]}
{"id": "36:14/q19", "question": "How did the king and townspeople finally respond?", "turns_on": "Conflicting narratives of the king's conversion and whether any townspeople survived as believers.", "positions": [{"id": "36:14/q19/p1", "position": "The king and some people believed; Gabriel's cry killed those who refused.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari and al-Baydawi say Simon's argument moved the king; al-Qurtubi says the revived boy's testimony led Simon to identify himself and the king and many believed. Al-Qushayri says the king believed but his people did not. Al-Nasafi includes Simon and the messengers among those who believed. Al-Tabataba'i's al-Ayyashi variant says the revived man was the king's son and king and people believed, though the destruction of unbelievers is recounted by other versions."}, {"id": "36:14/q19/p2", "position": "The king remained an unbeliever and joined his people in persecuting the envoys; the unbelievers were destroyed.", "reasons": "Wahb and Ka'b say the king and people continued torture and killing. Bursevi prefers this account: if king or subjects had believed they would have aided the envoys as Habib did, especially with clear proof and a population that follows its king. Ibn Ishaq also says the king resolved to kill them; Ibn Atiyya says the townspeople persisted and a heavenly cry silenced them."}]}
{"id": "36:14/q20", "question": "How did the envoys understand the townspeople's language?", "turns_on": "Different reported means of overcoming the language barrier.", "positions": [{"id": "36:14/q20/p1", "position": "God put them to sleep, angels carried them to Antioch, and they awoke speaking its language.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi links this wonder to God's strengthening Jesus with the Holy Spirit in 2:87 and 2:253."}, {"id": "36:14/q20/p2", "position": "An angel gave them luminous wine enabling comprehension of the local language.", "reasons": "Bursevi reports this from Kashf al-Asrar, alongside the claim that Jesus was told to dispatch apostles to cities before his ascension."}]}
{"id": "36:14/q21", "question": "Who spoke the declaration 'we are sent to you'?", "turns_on": "Whether the plural speech is simultaneous or a narrative summary of successive declarations.", "positions": [{"id": "36:14/q21/p1", "position": "All three messengers addressed the people together, or one spoke with the others' agreement.", "reasons": "Al-Tha'labi, al-Baghawi, al-Nasafi and Bursevi take the plural as the three. Al-Alusi allows plural attribution when one speaks for a concurring group. Bursevi says denial of the two amounts to denial of the third because their message is one. Islahi allows collective embassy language despite different ranks, making Moses primary, Aaron assisting and the believer preaching Moses's message."}, {"id": "36:14/q21/p2", "position": "The first two spoke before the third arrived, and the third spoke after them.", "reasons": "Yahya ibn Sallam reports this speaking sequence, although the verse gives a collective declaration after mentioning the reinforcement."}]}
{"id": "36:14/q22", "question": "What commission did they declare to the people?", "turns_on": "The breadth of mursalūn as 'messengers' or 'message bearers' and the reported content of their call.", "positions": [{"id": "36:14/q22/p1", "position": "They were sent to call the people to worship the one God, abandon idols, and accept guidance and faith.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari says they renounced idols; Abu al-Aliya says worship God without partner. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi report their replies to the king that God created him and his idols, does as He wills, rules as He chooses, and heals by His permission. Ibn Atiyya says the call was to guidance and faith; al-Biqa'i says the two announced faith in God. Al-Zajjaj and al-Qurtubi say their duty was clear delivery, not control of belief; Abu Hayyan says they entrust their truth to God. Muqatil's revived girl warned of forgiveness for acceptance and punishment for rejection."}, {"id": "36:14/q22/p2", "position": "The line can also be rendered 'we are message bearers unto you.'", "reasons": "Study Quran notes this translation for the declaration here and in 36:16."}]}
{"id": "36:14/q23", "question": "Why is this first declaration emphasized with innā, and how does it differ from the later claim?", "turns_on": "Whether the first utterance is truly initial information or already answers a request or denial.", "positions": [{"id": "36:14/q23/p1", "position": "The first claim begins with innā; after stronger denial, the later assertion adds lām and, in the fuller exchange, an oath.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan say the first is initial information and the later lām responds to denial. Al-Samin says plain denial receives inna whereas emphatic denial receives inna and lām; he distinguishes initial, requestive and denial contexts, and reports al-Kindi's point that the forms have distinct meanings, recalling his failed attempt to imitate the Quran at al-Ma'ida. Al-Suyuti lists other Quranic emphasis particles and says emphasis rises with doubt or denial; for Jesus's envoys, the later oath and lām follow stronger rejection. Bursevi says prior rejection explains the group's emphasis."}, {"id": "36:14/q23/p2", "position": "Calling the first speech merely 'initial' misclassifies a context in which the audience already seeks or denies proof.", "reasons": "Al-Samin rejects al-Shaykh's initial-versus-denial account for confusing requestive and initial contexts; he still holds that inna and the later lām mark different degrees of denial."}]}
{"id": "36:14/q24", "question": "What does this account teach about successive messengers and evidence?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:14/q24/p1", "position": "A messenger can be supported by another; simultaneous messengers may share a law, while successive arrivals require renewed miracle and law.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumi draws the permissibility of reinforcing one messenger with another and distinguishes shared versus successive commissions. Al-Biqa'i says God sends no messenger without signs that can bring belief, directly or through another; he cites Tufayl ibn Amr's light as an example of a requested sign."}]}
{"id": "36:14/q25", "question": "What agency rule is drawn from God's attribution of the dispatch?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:14/q25/p1", "position": "An authorized subagent is the principal's agent: the principal may remove him but the intervening agent may not.", "reasons": "Al-Razi and Bursevi apply this rule to Jesus's sending under God's command."}]}
{"id": "36:14/q26", "question": "Does an apostolic interpretation conflict with the saying that no prophet came between Jesus and Muhammad?", "turns_on": "Whether 'prophet' in the saying includes confirmation of an earlier law or only an independent new law.", "positions": [{"id": "36:14/q26/p1", "position": "On the apostles reading, the disciples were not prophets during or after Jesus's life.", "reasons": "Bursevi infers this from their status as Jesus's envoys and cites the Prophet's saying, 'There is no prophet between me and him,' taking 'him' as Jesus."}, {"id": "36:14/q26/p2", "position": "The saying may exclude only a prophet bringing an independent law, leaving a prophet who confirms prior law possible.", "reasons": "Bursevi explicitly allows this narrower sense of the cited saying."}]}
{"id": "36:14/q27", "question": "How does the verse connect to its surrounding account and to Muhammad's audience?", "turns_on": "Whether the passage is read chiefly as a historical warning, a typological confirmation of Muhammad, or a discourse sequence.", "positions": [{"id": "36:14/q27/p1", "position": "The town's rejection is a warning and consolation for Mu

hammad and his Meccan opponents.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi says the sending completes the parable and consoles the Prophet. Islahi says Quraysh should see that rejecting messengers, blaming signs, treating warning as bad luck and threatening them leads to destruction. Kuranyolu says it warns Muhammad's deniers and strengthens followers; Study Quran says Muhammad is told to give Quraysh an example of people who treated earlier bearers as they treat him. Al-Razi adds that rejection of envoys sent with God's leave is rejection of the one who sent them."}, {"id": "36:14/q27/p2", "position": "The third also suggests Muhammad's apostleship confirming and strengthening the missions of Moses and Jesus.", "reasons": "Elmalili prefers this representational aim and cites 2:97, 3:3 and 5:48."}, {"id": "36:14/q27/p3", "position": "The narrative unfolds through implied questions and answers throughout the passage.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjani reads the arrival, denial, threats and responses through this discourse pattern, comparing 15:57–58 and tracing it across 36:13, 15–17 and 19–20."}]}
{"id": "36:18/q01", "question": "What does تَطَيَّرْنَا بِكُمْ mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the speakers blame the envoys for their own misfortune or voice a prediction of punishment; Study Quran leaves the direction of the prediction open.", "positions": [{"id": "36:18/q01/p1", "position": "They regarded the messengers as a bad omen and attributed misfortune to them.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Yaḥyā, al-Ṭabarī, al-Zajjāj, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, al-Zamakhsharī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Biqāʿī, al-Ālūsī, al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī, Asad, Iṣlāḥī, and Study Quran give the basic sense. Qatāda says any evil that struck or would strike them was blamed on the envoys (Yaḥyā, ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Ibn Qutayba, al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Māwardī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Abū Ḥayyān, Ibn Kathīr, al-Durr). Ibn Kathīr says their arrival brought no good fortune. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and al-Ṭabrisī derive the verb from taking auguries from birds, favorable as well as unfavorable, though the verb commonly implies bad luck; al-Būrsawī specifies rightward flight as auspicious and leftward as ominous, then extension to every superstition. Al-Biqāʿī says the conspicuous, deliberate wording differs from 27:47 and 7:131."}, {"id": "36:18/q01/p2", "position": "They anticipated that people such as these messengers would bring punishment on the town.", "reasons": "Mujāhid, as transmitted by Ibn Kathīr, says that when such people enter a town, its inhabitants are punished. Study Quran also allows that the speakers foretell punishment to befall the messengers, a different direction for the anticipated harm."}]}
{"id": "36:18/q02", "question": "What prompted the townspeople's ill-omen claim?", "turns_on": "The notes identify different triggers: actual drought or leprosy, social discord, dislike of the call, or fear of its warning; Ibn ʿAṭiyya prefers discord.", "positions": [{"id": "36:18/q02/p1", "position": "Rain stopped and drought or related hardship was blamed on the messengers.", "reasons": "Muqātil gives withheld rain; al-Qurṭubī reports his duration as three years. Yaḥyā ibn Sallām in al-Māwardī locates the possible drought in Antioch. Al-Naqshbandī in al-Būrsawī adds that calamities began after the envoys arrived and the people told them to leave. Al-Biqāʿī mentions drought, hardship and other trials, explaining that the arrival of the righteous becomes blessing or punishment according to the community's response. Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Nasafī and others report this as one explanation."}, {"id": "36:18/q02/p2", "position": "They disliked the messengers' religion, message or apparent strangeness and treated what offended them as ominous.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī proposes aversion to the invited religion; al-Bayḍāwī says the message seemed strange, offensive and repellent; al-Nasafī ties it to dislike of their religion. Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Nasafī, al-Biqāʿī, al-Būrsawī and al-Ālūsī explain the ignorant habit of calling desired things auspicious and disliked things ominous even when real benefit and harm run otherwise. Al-Rāzī says the claim treats the envoys as a renewed cause of trouble and invokes the proverb that a false oath leaves homes desolate. Al-Ālūsī places the accusation after the opponents' arguments failed."}, {"id": "36:18/q02/p3", "position": "Preaching caused social division and turmoil in the town.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya judges this likeliest and compares Quraysh's omen about Muḥammad with the charge addressed to Moses. Abū Ḥayyān reports Ibn ʿAṭiyya's preference and cites 7:131 and 4:78. Al-Ālūsī says the wording implies the preaching triggered the discord."}, {"id": "36:18/q02/p4", "position": "Leprosy spread rapidly after they rejected the messengers.", "reasons": "Some interpreters in Ibn ʿAṭiyya report the outbreak; Abū Ḥayyān mentions increased leprosy, and al-Ālūsī transmits the report as an alternative to withheld rain."}, {"id": "36:18/q02/p5", "position": "They recoiled from the messengers' warning of harm if they did not believe.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī gives this as an alternative explanation of their fearful aversion to the call."}]}
{"id": "36:18/q03", "question": "What does the omen claim teach about superstition and good omens?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:18/q03/p1", "position": "Superstition attributes good or harm to what people favor or dislike; a good omen rests on good opinion of God.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Nasafī, al-Biqāʿī, al-Būrsawī and al-Ālūsī describe desire rather than actual good or harm driving these judgments. Al-Būrsawī says the Prophet liked good omens but disliked superstition because the former rests on good opinion of God and the latter relies on something besides Him. He reports the Prophet's exchange with Burayda ibn Aslam on the road to Medina: hearing Burayda's name, he told Abū Bakr their affair had cooled and gone well; hearing his lineage, he said they were safe from enemy plotting, using the wordplays برد أمرنا وصلح and سلمنا من كيدهم."}]}
{"id": "36:18/q04", "question": "What should someone do when an omen enters the heart?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:18/q04/p1", "position": "Affirm servitude to God and His power, deny that anything else brings good or removes evil, then proceed.", "reasons": "Al-Būrsawī cites a prophetic hadith prescribing these words and continuing one's course."}]}
{"id": "36:18/q05", "question": "What legal judgment is reported for acting on bird omens?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:18/q05/p1", "position": "Some jurists deem predicting death from a bird's cry, or turning back from travel because of one, unbelief.", "reasons": "Al-Būrsawī reports examples of an owl or other bird's cry taken to predict a patient's death and of a magpie's call causing a traveler to return."}]}
{"id": "36:18/q06", "question": "What must the messengers stop doing under لَئِن لَّمْ تَنتَهُوا?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:18/q06/p1", "position": "Stop claiming a divine mission and preaching to the town, especially speaking against its idols or religion.", "reasons": "Muqātil and Ibn al-Jawzī say to stop speaking; al-Ṭabarī specifies claiming to be sent and forbidding idol worship; al-Wāḥidī glosses the condition as simply ceasing; al-Bayḍāwī, al-Durr, al-Būrsawī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī specify preaching or delivering the message. Al-Būrsawī adds stopping this claim and falling silent about the people, with a Persian gloss of desisting from preaching. Al-Ālūsī says to stop making this statement, while al-Māwardī reports Qatāda's warning not to leave their religion. Al-Biqāʿī reports their demand that the envoys stop their summons."}]}
{"id": "36:18/q07", "question": "What force does the oath in لَئِن لَّمْ تَنتَهُوا add?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:18/q07/p1", "position": "The speakers swear they will persist in carrying out their threat if the call continues.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says they insist under oath that they will not relent. Al-Būrsawī expands it as 'By God, if you do not stop this claim.'"}]}

{"id": "36:18/q15", "question": "What comparable Qurʾānic omen claims illuminate this one?", "turns_on": "The notes compare different precedents rather than dispute the availability of those comparisons.", "positions": [{"id": "36:18/q15/p1", "position": "Pharaoh's people blamed Moses and his followers for hardship, though their calamities called them to heed.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī cites 7:131; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān compare Moses' opponents, and al-Ālūsī repeats Ibn ʿAṭiyya's link. {"id": "36:77/q06", "question": "Why say ٱلْإِنسَٰنُ instead of using a pronoun?", "turns_on": "Whether the general noun chiefly universalizes the rebuke or voices disgust at the Quraysh.", "positions": [{"id": "36:77/q06/p1", "position": "The noun exposes a trait of human nature, extending the rebuke beyond the immediate opponent.", "reasons": "Al-Irshād, cited by Bursevī, says a pronoun would obscure that denial concerns human beings as such; al-Ālūsī likewise emphasizes human nature; Ibn Kathīr and Bursevī apply the general wording to every denier, and al-Biqāʿī includes the original opponent within the species."}, {"id": "36:77/q06/p2", "position": "The broad noun expresses disgust at the Quraysh.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī connects the choice to the conduct of the Quraysh under discussion."}]}

Bursevī allows either that his quarrel is clear or that he makes his argument apparent; al-Ālūsī takes mubīn transitively, revealing inner thoughts. Al-Ālūsī says the nominal sentence indicates continuing dispute."}, {"id": "36:77/q11/p2", "position": "A mature person is articulate, discerning and able to formulate and express an argument.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī contrasts insignificant fluid with articulate agency and compares 43:18; al-Bayḍāwī and Abū Ḥayyān explain the capacity to express what is within. Al-Ālūsī reports this as an alternative reading in which mubīn is transitive. Asad cites Rāzī's treatment at 16:4 of khasīm as a high manifestation of rational speech; Ibn ʿAṭiyya notes first creation itself yields an articulate disputant."}]}
{"id": "36:77/q12", "question": "What does the human's change from drop to disputant teach about conduct?", "turns_on": "Whether the change is foregrounded as a rebuke of arrogant denial or a reminder of the gift of human capacities.", "positions": [{"id": "36:77/q12/p1", "position": "It rebukes denial of resurrection and the ingratitude and arrogance of using God-given powers against Him.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī and Ibn al-Jawzī say reflection on one's lowly origin should end the dispute. Al-Zamakhsharī stresses unbelief, baseness and the contradiction of arguing that lifeless bones cannot live when the disputant arose from lifeless matter; al-Nasafī and Abū Ḥayyān agree. Al-Qushayrī compares a trained archer turning on his teacher; al-Biqāʿī cites that poem, and Bursevī adds poetry about a pupil and a puppy biting its keeper. Al-Bayḍāwī calls denial repayment of an immense gift with disobedience. Iṣlāḥī links favors with gratitude and accountability. Kur'an Yolu says the human arrogantly judges Creator and Prophet by reason alone; Study Quran says he becomes his own adversary by ignoring his origin. Ibn Kathīr cites Aḥmad and Ibn Mājah's divine saying about late regret for charity at death."}, {"id": "36:77/q12/p2", "position": "The transformation also recalls God's favor in giving existence and the human ability to reason and dispute.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī describes the move from nonexistence to disputation as a favor; Ibn al-Jawzī reports this as an alternative. Al-Qushayrī lists proportioned limbs, reason and discrimination; al-Zamakhsharī, al-Bayḍāwī, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī describe the resulting articulate faculty. Asad relays Rāzī's account of it as the highest manifestation of rational speech."}]}
{"id": "36:77/q13", "question": "How does first creation from a drop support resurrection?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:77/q13/p1", "position": "The Creator who first brought a human from a tiny, lifeless origin can restore life after death.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī argues from first creation from nothing. Al-Qushayrī says revival is no harder than first creation and cites fire from green branches and the equivalence of creating a likeness; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls first creation itself revival after nonexistence. Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Nasafī and Abū Ḥayyān stress the contradiction in denying life for old bones despite one's lifeless origin. Al-Bayḍāwī calls restoration easier than first creation. Ibn Kathīr links the weak drop to 77:20–22 and 76:2; Study Quran cites creation texts 16:4, 18:37, 22:5, 35:11, 40:67, 53:46, 75:37, 76:2, 80:19, 32:8 and 77:20. Kur'an Yolu adds that Makkan pagans accepted God as cosmic Creator."}]}
{"id": "36:77/q14", "question": "Why did the Makkan polytheists mock resurrection?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:77/q14/p1", "position": "They resisted prophethood and resurrection to preserve established worship of other gods and sway their community.", "reasons": "Kur'an Yolu says mockery served to influence those around them."}]}
{"id": "36:77/q15", "question": "What inward life and death can this creation image suggest?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:77/q15/p1", "position": "God gives believing hearts life by gnosis, while desire and tyranny deaden unbelieving souls.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayrī parallels this with God's reviving souls after death and forming humans from sperm and birds from eggs."}]}
{"id": "36:77/q16", "question": "How does this verse connect to its context in Yā Sīn?", "turns_on": "Whether the contextual force is the renewed proof from human creation or consolation following the opponents' speech.", "positions": [{"id": "36:77/q16/p1", "position": "It resumes and sharpens the proof of resurrection after earlier signs of God's power and provision.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī points from change and encompassing knowledge at 36:68 to a clearer proof here. Al-Ālūsī links the two questions at 36:71 through inversion: God provided goods for gratitude, yet people disbelieve; He made people from lowly fluid for humility, yet they argue. {"id": "36:77/q17", "question": "What virtues of Yā Sīn are reported?", "turns_on": "The two reports promise different benefits.", "positions": [{"id": "36:77/q17/p1", "position": "Sincere recitation brings forgiveness and a reward like reciting the Qurʾān twenty-two times.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī attributes this to a report from the Prophet that also calls Yā Sīn the Qurʾān's heart."}, {"id": "36:77/q17/p2", "position": "Yā Sīn intercedes for its reciter and brings forgiveness to its listener.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī transmits this second Prophetic report without a grading."}]}
